title: Swimmer's Ear in Cabo: Ear Infection Relief on Vacation
description: Ear pain after swimming or snorkeling in Cabo? Signs of swimmer's ear, what helps, when to see a doctor, and a 24/7 house call at your hotel for $189 USD.
h1: Swimmer's ear and ear infections in Cabo: what to do on vacation
image_alt: English-speaking doctor and pharmacy support for travelers in Cabo San Lucas

intro: Pools, snorkeling trips, surf lessons and long afternoons in the ocean are a big part of a Los Cabos vacation — and so is the occasional earache that follows. Swimmer's ear is one of the most common reasons travelers call a doctor after a few days of water activities, especially kids and anyone who swims every day.

This guide explains how to tell swimmer's ear from other ear problems, what usually helps, the warning signs that need a doctor, and how to get an English-speaking doctor to your hotel, villa or yacht without losing a beach day.

p: Swimmer's ear (the medical name is otitis externa) is an infection or irritation of the outer ear canal — the tube between the outside of your ear and the eardrum. When water stays trapped in the canal for a long time, the skin softens and becomes easier for bacteria or fungi to grow in. Scratching the canal with fingers, cotton swabs or earbuds can make it worse.
p_after: It is different from a middle ear infection (behind the eardrum), which often follows a cold or sinus congestion and is more common in young children. Both can hurt, and only an exam can tell them apart with confidence — which matters, because they are not always treated the same way.

p: Swimmer's ear usually starts mild and gets worse over a day or two. Typical signs include:
list: Itching inside the ear canal
Pain that gets worse when you pull on the earlobe or press the small flap in front of the ear
Redness or swelling of the ear canal or outer ear
A feeling that the ear is full or plugged
Clear, cloudy or yellowish fluid draining from the ear
Muffled hearing on the affected side
p_after: With a middle ear infection, pain is often deeper and may come with fever, congestion or a recent cold. Babies and toddlers may pull at their ears, sleep poorly or seem unusually fussy.

sections.h2: Why it happens so often in Cabo
list: Lots of time in the water: daily pool swims, snorkeling at the bays, paddleboarding and surf lessons keep ears wet for hours.
Heat and humidity: warm, damp conditions in the summer and early fall help germs grow in a moist ear canal.
Pressure changes: flying in and diving can irritate ears that are already congested.
Earbuds and cotton swabs: both can scratch the delicate skin of the canal and push wax and water deeper.

sections.h2: What usually helps (and what to avoid)
p: For mild symptoms, these general steps help many people feel more comfortable while they arrange to see a doctor:
list: Keep the ear dry. Skip swimming and snorkeling until the ear is checked, and avoid getting water in it in the shower.
Dry gently after water. Tilt your head to let water drain, and dry the outer ear with a towel. A hair dryer on the coolest, lowest setting held well away from the ear can help.
Do not put anything inside the canal — no cotton swabs, fingers, bobby pins or earbuds.
Ask before using drops. Do not put any drops, oils or home remedies in an ear that is draining, very painful or may have a damaged eardrum. A doctor or pharmacist can tell you what is safe.
Ask about pain relief. Check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking any pain reliever, especially for children, during pregnancy or if you take other medication.
p_after: Swimmer's ear often needs prescription ear drops, and a doctor may need to gently clean the canal first so the treatment can work. Waiting several days with an infected ear usually means more pain and more days out of the water.

p: Call a doctor the same day if you or someone in your group has:
list: Ear pain that is getting worse or keeps you from sleeping
Fluid, pus or blood draining from the ear
Fever of 100.4°F (38°C) or higher with ear pain
Swelling or redness spreading to the outer ear, face or behind the ear
Noticeable hearing loss or a feeling the ear is completely blocked
Ear pain in a baby or young child, or in someone with diabetes or a weakened immune system
Symptoms that are not improving after two to three days, or that started after diving or a flight
p_after: Call 911 right away for a severe headache with stiff neck, high fever with confusion or extreme drowsiness, sudden weakness or drooping of one side of the face, severe dizziness with vomiting, or painful swelling behind the ear that pushes the ear forward. These can be signs of a more serious infection that needs emergency care.

sections.h2: How to protect your ears for the rest of the trip
list: Use well-fitting swim earplugs or a snug swim cap if you are prone to ear problems.
Tilt your head and gently dry your outer ears after every swim or shower.
Leave earwax alone — it helps protect the canal from water and germs.
Avoid cotton swabs and do not sleep with earbuds in.
If you have a cold or congestion, ask a doctor before diving or snorkeling deep.
Have kids take breaks out of the pool so their ears can dry between swims.
p_after: Feeling unwell in other ways too? Our guide on what to do if you get sick in Cabo covers the most common vacation illnesses and how to get help fast.

faq.q: Can I go swimming with swimmer's ear?
faq.a: It is best to keep the ear dry until a doctor has checked it and treatment has started. Swimming with an infected ear usually makes it more painful and slower to heal. Ask the doctor when it is safe to get back in the water.

faq.q: Can I fly home with an ear infection?
faq.a: Many people can, but pressure changes during a flight may be uncomfortable, especially with a middle ear infection or congestion. If you have a flight coming up, mention it during your visit so the doctor can advise you.

faq.q: How much does a doctor visit for an ear infection cost in Cabo?
faq.a: A house call to your hotel, villa or yacht is $189 USD, and a clinic consultation is $99 USD. You pay after the visit and receive an itemized invoice in English and USD for travel insurance.

faq.q: Can I buy ear drops at a pharmacy in Cabo?
faq.a: Pharmacies in Cabo carry many ear products, but the right one depends on whether the eardrum is intact and what type of infection you have. It is safest to have the ear examined first; we can deliver anything prescribed straight to your room.

faq.q: When is ear pain an emergency?
faq.a: Call 911 for a severe headache with stiff neck, high fever with confusion, facial weakness, severe dizziness with vomiting, or painful swelling behind the ear.
